title: Computer Vision
subtitle: From pixels and filters to CNNs, detectors and vision transformers, classical and modern, with Python labs and playgrounds
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course in computer vision covering both classical and modern techniques: images as data and colour spaces; convolution, blurring and the median filter; Sobel, Canny and Hough; keypoints, descriptors, RANSAC and homographies; thresholding, morphology and connected components; camera geometry, calibration and stereo depth; HOG, Haar cascades, bags of visual words and SVMs; convolutional networks, ResNet and transfer learning; detection with IoU and non-maximum suppression, YOLO and Mask R-CNN, and segmentation with U-Net; and vision transformers, CLIP, SAM and diffusion with a look at bias and responsible use. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus a convolution playground and an IoU and NMS lab.

chapters.title: Images as data

maps.title: Images
links: Image | is | A grid of pixels

summary: A digital image is a grid of pixels. A grayscale pixel is one number, usually 0 to 255; a colour pixel has three channels, red, green and blue. In code, an image is an array with a shape such as height by width by 3.

Computer vision asks a machine to extract meaning from such arrays: what is in the picture, where, how far, how it moves. It splits into classical methods, built from hand-designed filters and geometry, and modern methods that learn their filters from data.
Simple operations already do useful work: converting to gray, adjusting brightness, flipping, resizing and counting intensities in a histogram.

glossary.def: One element of an image: a number for gray, or several for colour.
One plane of an image, such as the red channel.
A count of how many pixels have each intensity.
A colour space with hue, saturation and value, closer to how people describe colour.
The number of pixels in the image, width by height.

keyPoints: Image = array of shape (H, W) or (H, W, 3).

items: ELI5. A picture on a screen is a huge grid of tiny coloured dots, and each dot is just a number. The computer only ever sees the numbers.

A camera sensor counts light at millions of little sites. Each site becomes a pixel, a number. Lay them in rows and columns and you have an image. To a program, a photograph is nothing but a big table of numbers, and every vision algorithm is a calculation on that table.

A grayscale image has one number per pixel, from zero for black to 255 for white. A colour image has three, one each for red, green and blue. We write its shape as height, width, channels. Rows come first, so pixel (r, c) is at row r down and column c across.

lesson.code:
import numpy as np
import cv2                     # OpenCV

img = cv2.imread('cat.jpg')     # BGR order in OpenCV!
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
print(img.shape, gray.shape)    # (480, 640, 3) (480, 640)
hist = cv2.calcHist([gray], [0], None, [256], [0, 256])
bright = np.clip(gray.astype(int) + 40, 0, 255).astype('uint8')

items: To turn colour into gray you average the channels, but not equally: the eye is most sensitive to green, so the standard weights are about 0.299 red, 0.587 green and 0.114 blue. Other colour spaces help other tasks.
HSV separates the hue, the actual colour, from how pale and how bright it is, which makes tasks like finding red objects easier.

A histogram counts how many pixels have each brightness. A dark, low-contrast photo has all its counts bunched at the left. Stretching the histogram, or equalising it, spreads the values and boosts contrast.
Brightness adjustment is addition with clipping to the range 0 to 255, so values do not wrap around.

This course follows the history of the field. First the classical toolkit of filters, edges, corners, segmentation and geometry, which still powers phones, factories and robots. Then convolutional networks, detection and segmentation, vision transformers and foundation models.
The labs build the main ideas in plain Python on small images, so you see every step.

practice.title: Brightness
practice.intro: Write brighten(img, delta): add delta to every pixel of a gray image and clip each result to 0..255.
practice.solution:
def brighten(img, delta):
    return [[max(0, min(255, v + delta)) for v in row] for row in img]

practice.title: Flip and rotate
practice.intro: Write rot90(img): rotate a gray image (list of rows) 90 degrees clockwise.
practice.hint: Column c of the result is column c read bottom to top.
practice.solution:
def rot90(img):
    h = len(img)
    w = len(img[0])
    out = []
    for c in range(w):
        out.append([img[h - 1 - r][c] for r in range(h)])
    return out

practice.title: Resize (nearest neighbour)
practice.intro: Write resize(img, new_h, new_w): nearest-neighbour resize: output pixel (r, c) takes img[r * h // new_h][c * w // new_w] where h, w are the original sizes.
practice.hint: Map each output pixel back to the source.
practice.solution:
def resize(img, new_h, new_w):
    h = len(img)
    w = len(img[0])
    return [[img[r * h // new_h][c * w // new_w] for c in range(new_w)] for r in range(new_h)]

practice.title: Value channel (HSV)
practice.intro: Write rgb_to_hsv(r, g, b) for 0..255 channels: return [hue in degrees 0..360 rounded to 1 decimal, saturation 0..1 rounded to 3, value 0..1 rounded to 3]. Hue is 0 when max equals min.
practice.hint: Use the max channel to pick the hue branch.
practice.solution:
def rgb_to_hsv(r, g, b):
    r1 = r / 255.0
    g1 = g / 255.0
    b1 = b / 255.0
    mx = max(r1, g1, b1)
    mn = min(r1, g1, b1)
    d = mx - mn
    if d == 0:
        h = 0.0
    elif mx == r1:
        h = 60.0 * (((g1 - b1) / d) % 6)
    elif mx == g1:
        h = 60.0 * ((b1 - r1) / d + 2)
    else:
        h = 60.0 * ((r1 - g1) / d + 4)
    s = 0.0 if mx == 0 else d / mx
    return [round(h, 1), round(s, 3), round(mx, 3)]

chapters.title: Filtering and convolution

maps.title: Filtering
links: Kernel | is | A small weight grid
Median filter | removes | Salt and pepper

summary: A filter replaces each pixel by a weighted sum of its neighbours. The weights form a small grid called a kernel, and sliding it over the image is convolution (or its twin, correlation).

A box blur averages; a Gaussian blur weights nearer pixels more and blurs without blocky artefacts; sharpening subtracts a blur from the original to boost detail. A median filter, which is not linear, removes isolated speckles without smearing edges.
Many kernels are separable: a 2D Gaussian is the product of two 1D ones, which cuts the work from k squared to 2k per pixel.

glossary.def: A small grid of weights applied around each pixel.
Sliding a (flipped) kernel over an image and summing products at each position.
A smoothing filter whose weights follow a bell curve.
Replaces each pixel with the median of its neighbourhood.
A 2D kernel that is the outer product of two 1D kernels.

keyPoints: Gaussian sigma sets the blur size.
Median removes salt and pepper noise.

items: ELI5. To blur a photo, every dot is mixed with its neighbours. The recipe for mixing is a little table of numbers called a kernel.

To blur a photo, replace each pixel by the average of itself and its eight neighbours. To sharpen it, push each pixel away from the average of its neighbours. Both are the same operation with different numbers.
The numbers form a kernel, a little 3 by 3 table, and the operation is called convolution.

Strictly, convolution flips the kernel before sliding, while correlation does not. Deep learning libraries actually compute correlation and call it convolution. For symmetric kernels, such as blurs, there is no difference.
The output is a new image, smaller by the kernel's border unless the edges are padded with zeros or copies.

lesson.code:
import cv2, numpy as np
blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (5, 5), sigmaX=1.2)
k = np.array([[0, -1, 0], [-1, 5, -1], [0, -1, 0]], dtype=np.float32)
sharp = cv2.filter2D(img, -1, k)
clean = cv2.medianBlur(noisy, 3)

items: The Gaussian kernel is the natural blur. Its weights fall off like a bell curve with distance, with a parameter sigma that sets how wide it is. A larger sigma gives a stronger blur.
Because the 2D Gaussian equals a product of two 1D bell curves, you can blur rows then columns, which is much cheaper for big kernels.
Noise comes in kinds. Gaussian noise is small random variation everywhere, and blurring reduces it, at the cost of detail. Salt-and-pepper noise is isolated white and black dots.
Blurring merely smears them, but a median filter, taking the middle value of the neighbourhood, removes them cleanly and keeps edges sharp. The playground lets you try kernels on a test image.

practice.title: Gaussian kernel
practice.intro: Write gaussian_kernel(size, sigma): a size x size kernel (size odd) with weights exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / (2 sigma^2)) where x, y are offsets from the centre, normalised to sum to 1, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def gaussian_kernel(size, sigma):
    c = size // 2
    k = []
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(size):
        row = []
        for j in range(size):
            v = math.exp(-((i - c) ** 2 + (j - c) ** 2) / (2.0 * sigma * sigma))
            row.append(v)
            total = total + v
        k.append(row)
    return [[round(v / total, 4) for v in row] for row in k]

chapters.title: Edges, gradients and lines
summary: An edge is a place where brightness changes quickly. The gradient of an image points in the direction of fastest increase and its length measures how fast; edges are where the gradient magnitude is large.

The Sobel kernels estimate the horizontal and vertical derivatives. The Canny detector smooths, finds the gradient, thins edges to one pixel by non-maximum suppression and links them with two thresholds.
The Hough transform finds lines by letting every edge pixel vote for all the lines that could pass through it; real lines collect many votes.

glossary.def: A vector of partial derivatives (dI/dx, dI/dy) pointing to the steepest increase.
A pair of 3x3 kernels that approximate the x and y derivatives with some smoothing.
Keeping only pixels that are local maxima along the gradient direction, to thin edges.
Keeping strong edges and weak edges only if connected to strong ones.
A voting method that detects shapes, such as lines, in a parameter space.

keyPoints: Line: rho = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta).

items: ELI5. An edge is where the picture changes suddenly, like the outline of a cup against a table. We find it by looking for big jumps between neighbours.

Where does one object end and another begin? Often at an edge: a sudden jump in brightness. In calculus a jump is a large derivative, so edge detection is derivative estimation. For an image we have two derivatives, left to right and top to bottom, and together they make the gradient.

A derivative is a difference between neighbours. The Sobel kernels do this over a 3 by 3 patch and also smooth a little, which tames noise. One kernel responds to vertical edges, the other to horizontal.
Combine their outputs as the square root of the sum of squares to get the strength of the edge in any direction, and take the arctangent to get its orientation.

lesson.code:
gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
mag = np.hypot(gx, gy)
edges = cv2.Canny(gray, 100, 200)
lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(edges, 1, np.pi/180, threshold=80,
                        minLineLength=50, maxLineGap=10)

items: A thick band of strong gradient is not yet an edge map. John Canny's 1986 detector adds three ideas. Blur first to resist noise. Thin the band to a single pixel line by keeping only local maxima across the edge.
Then use two thresholds: strong pixels are certainly edges, weak ones count only if they connect to a strong one. This gives clean continuous contours and the method is still widely used.

Edges are fragments; we often want lines, circles or other shapes. The Hough transform turns detection into voting. A line through the origin at angle theta is described by its distance rho. Each edge pixel votes for every pair of values rho and theta consistent with a line through it.
Votes pile up for the true lines. The method tolerates gaps and noise, and the lab runs it on a handful of points.

practice.title: Sobel gradients
practice.intro: Write sobel(img): for the valid 3x3 positions return [Gx, Gy] where Gx is the sum of the kernel [[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]] times the patch and Gy the same with the transposed kernel [[-1,-2,-1],[0,0,0],[1,2,1]]. Return two images (lists of rows): [Gx_image, Gy_image].
practice.solution:
def sobel(img):
    kx = [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
    ky = [[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]]
    h = len(img)
    w = len(img[0])
    gx = []
    gy = []
    for r in range(h - 2):
        rx = []
        ry = []
        for c in range(w - 2):
            sx = 0
            sy = 0
            for i in range(3):
                for j in range(3):
                    sx = sx + kx[i][j] * img[r + i][c + j]
                    sy = sy + ky[i][j] * img[r + i][c + j]
            rx.append(sx)
            ry.append(sy)
        gx.append(rx)
        gy.append(ry)
    return [gx, gy]

chapters.title: Features, matching and geometry of images
summary: To recognise a place or stitch photos we need points that can be found again from another view. Corners are good: the image changes in every direction around them. The Harris detector scores this with the structure tensor.

A descriptor summarises the patch around a keypoint as a vector. SIFT uses gradient histograms; ORB uses a binary string compared with Hamming distance. Matching finds nearest descriptors and a ratio test removes ambiguous ones.
RANSAC fits a model, such as a homography, to many noisy matches by repeatedly fitting to random minimal sets and keeping the model with the most inliers.

glossary.def: A distinctive, repeatable image location such as a corner.
A vector describing the appearance around a keypoint, used for matching.
Accepting a match only if the best distance is much smaller than the second-best.
Random sample consensus: fit models to random subsets and keep the one agreeing with most data.
A 3x3 matrix mapping points between two views of a plane.

keyPoints: ORB descriptor: bits; compare with Hamming distance.
RANSAC: sample, fit, count inliers, repeat.

items: ELI5. Some spots in a picture, like corners, are easy to recognise again from another angle, like the corner of a window. We pick those spots to match two photos.

Stand in front of a blank wall and you cannot tell where you are looking. Stand in front of a window frame and you can. Corners and blobs are distinctive: shift a small window around them and the picture changes in every direction. The Harris detector measures exactly that.
From the image gradients in a window it forms a small 2 by 2 matrix; a corner makes both of its eigenvalues large, an edge only one, and a flat patch none.

Finding a keypoint is half the job. To match it in another photo we describe its neighbourhood with a vector that survives changes in rotation, scale and lighting. SIFT, from David Lowe, builds histograms of gradient directions.
ORB makes a string of brightness comparisons between pixel pairs, a binary descriptor that can be compared with the Hamming distance, the count of differing bits, extremely fast.

lesson.code:
orb = cv2.ORB_create(1000)
k1, d1 = orb.detectAndCompute(img1, None)
k2, d2 = orb.detectAndCompute(img2, None)
bf = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING)
matches = bf.knnMatch(d1, d2, k=2)
good = [m for m, n in matches if m.distance < 0.75 * n.distance]
pts1 = np.float32([k1[m.queryIdx].pt for m in good])
pts2 = np.float32([k2[m.trainIdx].pt for m in good])
H, mask = cv2.findHomography(pts1, pts2, cv2.RANSAC, 5.0)

items: Matching is never perfect: repeated windows and textures create ambiguous matches. Lowe's ratio test keeps a match only when the best candidate is clearly closer than the second best.
Some wrong matches still remain, and a method that fits a line or homography by least squares would be dragged away by them. RANSAC is the cure.

RANSAC picks the minimum number of matches needed for the model, two for a line, four for a homography, fits it, and counts how many other matches agree within a tolerance, the inliers. After many random trials, it keeps the model with the most inliers and refits on them.
A homography is the 3 by 3 matrix describing how a flat surface looks from two viewpoints, which is the basis of panorama stitching, document scanning and augmented reality.

practice.title: Hamming distance
practice.intro: Write hamming(a, b): the number of differing bits between two integers.
practice.solution:
def hamming(a, b):
    x = a ^ b
    n = 0
    while x:
        n = n + (x & 1)
        x = x >> 1
    return n

chapters.title: Segmentation, morphology and regions
summary: Segmentation divides an image into meaningful regions. The simplest method is thresholding: pixels above a value are foreground. Otsu's method picks the threshold that best separates the two groups of the histogram.
Morphological operations clean up binary masks: erosion shrinks shapes and removes specks, dilation grows them and fills holes, and opening and closing combine the two.
Connected component labelling counts and measures blobs. Clustering colours with k-means and the watershed algorithm are other classical ways to segment.

glossary.def: Splitting pixels into two classes by comparing intensity with a value.
A way to choose a threshold by maximising the variance between the two resulting classes.
Shrinking foreground shapes: a pixel stays only if all its neighbours are foreground.
Growing foreground shapes: a pixel turns on if any neighbour is foreground.
Maximal sets of foreground pixels connected to each other.

items: ELI5. To count coins, turn the picture into black and white, tidy up the specks, and count the white blobs.

Count the coins on a table, find the tumour in a scan, cut a person out of a photo. All start with segmentation: deciding which pixels belong together. The simplest idea is a threshold. If coins are bright and the table is dark, mark every pixel above some value as coin.
But which value? Look at the histogram. If there are two humps, one for the dark background and one for the bright objects, the best threshold sits in the valley.
Otsu's method finds it automatically by trying every threshold and keeping the one that makes the two groups most different from each other, measured by the variance between the classes.

lesson.code:
_, mask = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
kernel = np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8)
clean = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)
n, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(clean)
print('objects:', n - 1)

items: Thresholding leaves noisy masks: stray dots and little holes. Morphological operations use a small shape, the structuring element, to tidy up. Erosion keeps a pixel only if the whole neighbourhood is foreground, so it removes specks and shrinks shapes.
Dilation turns a pixel on if any neighbour is on, so it grows shapes and closes gaps. Erosion followed by dilation, called opening, removes specks without changing big shapes.

Then label the blobs. Connected component analysis scans the mask and gives each group of touching foreground pixels its own number, by flood filling from each unvisited pixel. The count gives the number of coins and the statistics give each one's area and centre.
Touching coins merge into one blob, which is where the watershed algorithm, treating the image as a landscape to flood from markers, can split them.

practice.title: Threshold
practice.intro: Write threshold(img, t): 1 where the pixel is greater than t, else 0.
practice.solution:
def threshold(img, t):
    return [[1 if v > t else 0 for v in row] for row in img]

practice.title: Otsu threshold
practice.intro: Write otsu(hist): for a histogram (list of counts per intensity level, at least 2 levels), return the threshold t (levels 0..t are background) that maximises the between-class variance w0 w1 (m0 - m1)^2. The first t wins ties.
practice.solution:
def otsu(hist):
    total = float(sum(hist))
    best = 0
    bv = -1.0
    for t in range(len(hist) - 1):
        w0 = sum(hist[:t + 1]) / total
        w1 = 1 - w0
        if w0 == 0 or w1 == 0:
            continue
        m0 = sum([i * hist[i] for i in range(t + 1)]) / (w0 * total)
        m1 = sum([i * hist[i] for i in range(t + 1, len(hist))]) / (w1 * total)
        v = w0 * w1 * (m0 - m1) ** 2
        if v > bv + 1e-9:
            bv = v
            best = t
    return best

chapters.title: Cameras, geometry and depth
summary: The pinhole model projects a 3D point (X, Y, Z) to the image at (f X / Z, f Y / Z): farther things appear smaller. Intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point) describe the camera; extrinsics give its position and rotation.
Real lenses distort straight lines; calibration with a checkerboard estimates the parameters so we can undo it.
Two cameras a baseline B apart see the same point shifted by a disparity d; depth is Z = f B / d. Closer objects have larger disparity.

glossary.def: An idealised camera in which light passes through a single point, projecting 3D points to the image plane.
The distance from the pinhole to the image plane, here in pixels, setting the field of view.
Estimating a camera's intrinsic parameters and lens distortion, often from images of a checkerboard.
The horizontal shift of a point between the left and right images of a stereo pair.
The geometry relating two views: a point in one image lies on a known line in the other.

keyPoints: u = f X / Z + cx; v = f Y / Z + cy.
Homogeneous coordinates make projection a matrix product.

items: ELI5. A camera squashes the 3D world flat. Things far away look small, and two eyes, or two cameras, can tell how far by how much things shift.

Hold a coin at arm's length and it covers a mountain. Distant things look small; the camera loses the third dimension and keeps a perspective view. The pinhole model captures this simply: a point at depth Z, X sideways, lands on the image at f times X over Z, where f is the focal length.
Double the distance and the image halves.

To use the model in practice we need the camera's numbers. Intrinsic parameters are the focal length in pixels and the principal point, where the optical axis meets the sensor. Extrinsic parameters say where the camera is and which way it points. Together they form the camera matrix.
Lenses also bend straight lines, so calibration images of a checkerboard let software estimate the distortion and correct it.

lesson.code:
ok, K, dist, rvecs, tvecs = cv2.calibrateCamera(obj_points, img_points, gray.shape[::-1], None, None)
undistorted = cv2.undistort(img, K, dist)

stereo = cv2.StereoSGBM_create(minDisparity=0, numDisparities=64, blockSize=7)
disp = stereo.compute(left_gray, right_gray).astype('float32') / 16.0
depth = f * baseline / np.maximum(disp, 0.1)

items: Depth comes from two views. Hold a finger in front of you and close one eye then the other: the finger jumps against the background. That jump, the disparity, is large for close things and small for far ones.

With two cameras a baseline B apart and focal length f, a point with disparity d lies at depth Z equal to f B over d. Finding the matching pixel in the other image, stereo matching, is a search along one row after rectification.

Modern systems also estimate depth from a single image with learned models, or measure it directly with LiDAR and time-of-flight sensors. Structure from motion and SLAM combine many views, solving for camera poses and 3D points together, which is how phones and robots build maps.
The labs project points, triangulate depth and apply transforms.

chapters.title: Classical recognition: HOG, Haar and bags of features

maps.title: Recognition
links: Bag of words | counts | Visual words

summary: Before deep learning, recognition was a pipeline: extract hand-designed features, then train a classifier. HOG (histogram of oriented gradients) describes shape by local gradient directions and, with a linear SVM, detected pedestrians.
Viola and Jones detected faces in real time using Haar features (differences of rectangle sums) computed instantly from an integral image, and a cascade that rejects most windows early.
Bag of visual words clusters local descriptors into a vocabulary and describes an image by the histogram of words, then classifies the histogram.

glossary.def: Histogram of oriented gradients: a descriptor built from gradient-direction histograms in cells.
An image where each entry holds the sum of all pixels above and to the left, allowing any rectangle sum in four lookups.
The difference between the sums of pixels in adjacent rectangles.
A sequence of classifiers in which early cheap stages reject most non-objects.
A classifier that finds the separating boundary with the widest margin.

keyPoints: Rectangle sum = I(D) - I(B) - I(C) + I(A).
Sliding window x image pyramid = detector.
Bag of words: histogram of cluster ids.

items: ELI5. Before computers could learn, people wrote rules like 'faces have two dark eyes above a lighter cheek band' and checked millions of little windows quickly.

Early face detectors seemed impossible in real time. Paul Viola and Michael Jones solved it in 2001 with three ideas. First, simple features: Haar-like rectangles, such as a dark band across the eyes above a lighter band on the cheeks.
Second, the integral image, which lets you add up any rectangle with just four array lookups. Third, a cascade of classifiers, so that most windows are rejected by the first cheap tests.

The integral image is a lovely trick. Make a table where each entry is the sum of all pixels above and to the left of it. The sum over any rectangle is then the bottom-right entry, minus the entries to the left and above, plus the corner that was subtracted twice. Constant time, whatever the size.
The feature value is a difference of two or three such sums.

Another classic, HOG by Navneet Dalal and Bill Triggs, describes an object by its edges. Divide the window into cells of 8 by 8 pixels. In each cell, build a histogram of gradient directions weighted by gradient strength. Normalise over blocks of cells for lighting invariance.
A linear support vector machine trained on these long vectors detects pedestrians well, and the whole pipeline slides across the image at many scales.

lesson.code:
from skimage.feature import hog
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC

feat = hog(gray, orientations=9, pixels_per_cell=(8, 8), cells_per_block=(2, 2))
clf = LinearSVC(C=0.01).fit(train_features, train_labels)

face = cv2.CascadeClassifier(cv2.data.haarcascades + 'haarcascade_frontalface_default.xml')
boxes = face.detectMultiScale(gray, scaleFactor=1.1, minNeighbors=5)

items: For whole-image categories such as 'beach' or 'forest', the bag of visual words treats local descriptors like words in a document. Cluster thousands of SIFT descriptors with k-means; each centre is a visual word.

Describe an image by the histogram of words it contains and train an SVM on histograms. These pipelines dominated until 2012, when learned features overtook them, but their ideas, sliding windows, multiscale pyramids and normalisation, live on in modern detectors.

practice.title: HOG cell histogram
practice.intro: Write hog_cell(gx, gy, bins): for equal-length lists of gradient components of a cell, build an unsigned-orientation histogram: orientation = atan2(gy, gx) in degrees folded into [0, 180), bin width 180 / bins, each pixel adds its magnitude sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2) to its bin. Return the histogram rounded to 2 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def hog_cell(gx, gy, bins):
    hist = [0.0] * bins
    w = 180.0 / bins
    for i in range(len(gx)):
        ang = math.degrees(math.atan2(gy[i], gx[i])) % 180.0
        mag = math.sqrt(gx[i] ** 2 + gy[i] ** 2)
        b = int(ang // w)
        if b >= bins:
            b = bins - 1
        hist[b] = hist[b] + mag
    return [round(v, 2) for v in hist]

chapters.title: Convolutional neural networks
summary: A convolutional neural network stacks learned convolution layers with non-linearities and pooling. Early layers learn edges, middle layers textures and parts, late layers whole objects.
AlexNet's win in the 2012 ImageNet contest started the deep learning era. VGG, Inception and ResNet followed; ResNet's skip connections made very deep networks trainable.
Instead of training from scratch, you usually start from a network pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tune it on your own data: transfer learning.

glossary.def: A layer applying many learned small kernels across the image, sharing weights across positions.
Downsampling feature maps, for example by taking the maximum of each 2x2 block.
The region of the input image that influences a given unit.
A shortcut that adds a layer's input to its output, as in ResNet.
Starting from a model trained on a large dataset and adapting it to a new task.

keyPoints: Params per conv layer = K*K*Cin*Cout + Cout.
Max pool 2x2 halves width and height.
Fine-tune: freeze early layers, train the head.

items: ELI5. A neural network for pictures learns its own little tables, first for edges, then for shapes, then for whole animals.

In classical vision, experts designed the filters. A convolutional network lets the data decide. It stacks layers in which many small kernels slide over the image, exactly the convolution of Chapter 2, but with the numbers in each kernel learned by gradient descent.
Sharing each kernel across all positions makes the network efficient and gives it translation equivariance: a cat is a cat wherever it sits.

A typical block is convolution, a non-linearity such as ReLU, and pooling. Pooling shrinks the maps, say taking the biggest value in each 2 by 2 block, so deeper layers see wider regions of the image: the receptive field grows.
Peering inside trained networks shows early layers responding to edges and colours, middle layers to textures and parts like eyes and wheels, and the last layers to whole objects.

lesson.code:
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers

model = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Input((64, 64, 3)),
    layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation='relu'), layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation='relu'), layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    layers.Flatten(), layers.Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax'),
])
base = keras.applications.ResNet50(weights='imagenet', include_top=False)
base.trainable = False   # transfer learning: train only a new head

items: The ImageNet contest asked programs to classify a million photographs into a thousand categories. In 2012, AlexNet, a deep CNN trained on graphics cards, cut the error from twenty-six to sixteen percent, and the field changed.

Deeper networks followed, but stacking layers eventually made training harder. ResNet's fix in 2015 was the skip connection: each block learns a residual, a correction added to its input, so the signal and gradient pass straight through. Networks with over a hundred layers trained well.

Training a large CNN from scratch needs millions of images. Transfer learning avoids that. Take a network pretrained on ImageNet, replace its last layer with one for your classes, and train just that layer, or fine-tune the whole network gently. A few hundred examples can be enough.
Data augmentation, random flips, crops and colour changes, stretches small datasets further. Count the sizes and parameters in the labs; it shows why convolution is so economical.

practice.title: Max pool
practice.intro: Write max_pool(img, size): non-overlapping size x size max pooling (stride = size); incomplete blocks at the edges are ignored.

practice.title: Strided convolution
practice.intro: Write conv_stride(img, k, stride, pad): zero-pad the image by pad on all sides, then slide the kernel k with the given stride (no flip) and return the output image.
practice.hint: Pad, then step by the stride.
practice.solution:
def conv_stride(img, k, stride, pad):
    h = len(img)
    w = len(img[0])
    P = [[0] * (w + 2 * pad) for _ in range(h + 2 * pad)]
    for r in range(h):
        for c in range(w):
            P[r + pad][c + pad] = img[r][c]
    kh = len(k)
    kw = len(k[0])
    out = []
    r = 0
    while r + kh <= len(P):
        row = []
        c = 0
        while c + kw <= len(P[0]):
            s = 0
            for i in range(kh):
                for j in range(kw):
                    s = s + k[i][j] * P[r + i][c + j]
            row.append(s)
            c = c + stride
        out.append(row)
        r = r + stride
    return out

practice.title: Receptive field
practice.intro: Write receptive_field(layers): layers is a list of [kernel, stride]; return the receptive field of one unit in the last layer using rf = 1, jump = 1; for each layer rf += (k - 1) x jump, jump *= stride.
practice.solution:
def receptive_field(layers):
    rf = 1
    jump = 1
    for k, s in layers:
        rf = rf + (k - 1) * jump
        jump = jump * s
    return rf

practice.title: Residual block
practice.intro: Write residual(x, f_out): the elementwise sum x + f_out of the input vector and the layer's output (equal lengths); then return the ReLU of the sum.
practice.solution:
def residual(x, f_out):
    return [max(0, x[i] + f_out[i]) for i in range(len(x))]

chapters.title: Detection, segmentation and tracking
summary: Detection finds what and where: a box and a class for every object. Intersection over union (IoU) measures how well two boxes overlap, and non-maximum suppression removes duplicate detections of the same object.
R-CNN families propose regions then classify them; YOLO and SSD predict boxes in a single pass and run in real time. Mask R-CNN adds a mask per object (instance segmentation).
Semantic segmentation labels every pixel; encoder-decoder networks such as U-Net downsample to understand and upsample to localise.

glossary.def: A rectangle that encloses an object, given by its corners or by centre, width and height.
The area of overlap of two boxes divided by the area of their union.
Discarding boxes that overlap a higher-scoring box of the same class too much.
Finding each object and giving it a pixel mask.
A standard detection score averaging precision over recall levels and classes.

keyPoints: NMS: sort by score, keep, drop IoU > threshold.

items: ELI5. To find all the cars in a photo, the computer draws boxes, scores them, and throws away boxes that sit on top of better ones.

Classifying a photograph as 'street' is one thing; finding every car, pedestrian and traffic light in it, with boxes, is detection, and self-driving cars depend on it. A detector outputs, for each object, a box, a class and a confidence score.

To judge a box we need a measure of overlap. Intersection over union divides the area the predicted and true boxes share by the area they cover together. One is a perfect match, zero is no overlap, and a detection is usually counted correct if its IoU with a true box is at least one half.
Detectors often fire many overlapping boxes on one object, so non-maximum suppression sorts boxes by score, keeps the best, and deletes any other box that overlaps it too much.

lesson.code:
from ultralytics import YOLO
model = YOLO('yolov8n.pt')
results = model('street.jpg')
for box in results[0].boxes:
    print(box.cls, box.conf, box.xyxy)

import torchvision
mask_rcnn = torchvision.models.detection.maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights='DEFAULT').eval()

items: Two families of detector dominate. The R-CNN family first proposes regions that might contain objects, then classifies and refines each; Faster R-CNN made proposals part of the network.

YOLO, short for you only look once, and SSD divide the image into a grid and predict boxes and classes for every cell in one forward pass, fast enough for video. Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a mask for each detected object.

Sometimes boxes are not enough and we need a label for every pixel: road, sky, person. That is semantic segmentation. U-Net, shaped like the letter U, downsamples through convolutions to capture context and then upsamples back to full size, with skip connections carrying fine detail across.

It became the standard for medical images. Add tracking across video frames, linking boxes by IoU and appearance, and you have the core of modern perception systems. The playground lets you drag boxes and see IoU and suppression.

practice.title: IoU
practice.intro: Write iou(a, b): the IoU of two boxes [x1, y1, x2, y2] (x1 < x2, y1 < y2), rounded to 4 decimals; 0 if they do not overlap.
practice.solution:
def iou(a, b):
    x1 = max(a[0], b[0])
    y1 = max(a[1], b[1])
    x2 = min(a[2], b[2])
    y2 = min(a[3], b[3])
    w = x2 - x1
    h = y2 - y1
    if w <= 0 or h <= 0:
        return 0
    inter = w * h
    ua = (a[2] - a[0]) * (a[3] - a[1]) + (b[2] - b[0]) * (b[3] - b[1]) - inter
    return round(inter / float(ua), 4)

chapters.title: Vision transformers, foundation models and responsible vision
summary: The Vision Transformer (ViT) cuts an image into patches, treats each as a token, adds position information and applies self-attention so every patch can relate to every other. With enough data it matches or beats CNNs.

Foundation models are trained on huge data and reused for many tasks. CLIP learns to match images with captions, enabling zero-shot classification by comparing an image with text prompts. SAM segments any object from a click or a box.
Diffusion models generate images by learning to remove noise step by step. These powerful tools also raise issues of bias, privacy, surveillance and misinformation.

glossary.def: A model that splits an image into patches and processes them as a sequence with a transformer.
A mechanism in which each token computes a weighted average of all tokens' values, with weights from query-key similarity.
A model trained to place images and their captions near each other in a shared embedding space.
Classifying into categories never trained on, by comparing the image with text descriptions of the classes.
A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process.

keyPoints: CLIP: cosine similarity of image and text embeddings.
Diffusion: x_t = sqrt(a) x_0 + sqrt(1 - a) noise.

items: ELI5. New models cut a photo into small squares and let every square look at every other, and some learn pictures and words together so they can name things they were never taught.
For a decade convolutional networks ruled vision. Then in 2020 researchers at Google showed that a plain transformer, the architecture behind language models, could classify images just as well.
The trick is to chop the image into patches, say 16 by 16 pixels, flatten each into a vector and treat the patches as the words of a sentence. A 224 by 224 image becomes 196 tokens.

The transformer's key operation is self-attention. Every patch asks a question, a query, and every patch offers a key; the match between a query and a key decides how much that patch's value contributes to the answer.
The result is that any patch can directly draw on any other, even far away, while a convolution only sees its small neighbourhood. Positional embeddings tell the model where each patch sat.

lesson.code:
from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor
from PIL import Image

model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained('openai/clip-vit-base-patch32')
proc = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained('openai/clip-vit-base-patch32')
image = Image.open('photo.jpg')
texts = ['a photo of a dog', 'a photo of a cat', 'a photo of a bicycle']
inputs = proc(text=texts, images=image, return_tensors='pt', padding=True)
probs = model(**inputs).logits_per_image.softmax(dim=1)
print(probs)

items: Large pretrained 'foundation' models changed practice. CLIP was trained on hundreds of millions of image and caption pairs to place matching pairs close together.

To classify with no extra training, you write a sentence for each class, embed them, and pick the one nearest the image: zero-shot classification. The Segment Anything Model segments any object you point at. DINO-style self-supervised models learn useful features from images alone.

Generation, too, is learned. Diffusion models gradually add noise to training images until nothing remains, and train a network to undo one step of that noise. To create a picture, begin with pure noise and repeatedly denoise, optionally guided by a text prompt.

The same power raises serious questions: face recognition and surveillance, bias when training data under-represents groups, deepfakes and consent. Audit models across groups, document their limits, and ask whether a system should be built at all.

lesson.title: Key terms at a glance
head: Term
Meaning
rows: Vision Transformer
A model that splits an image into patches and processes them as a sequence with a transformer.
Self-attention

practice.title: Number of tokens
practice.intro: Write num_tokens(h, w, p): how many patches an h x w image gives with patch size p, assuming divisibility.
practice.hint: Count patches per row and column.
practice.solution:
def num_tokens(h, w, p):
    return (h // p) * (w // p)

practice.title: Attention weights
practice.intro: Write attention(q, keys): the softmax over keys of the scaled dot product q.k / sqrt(d), where d is the length of q. Return the weights rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def attention(q, keys):
    d = len(q)
    scores = []
    for k in keys:
        s = 0.0
        for j in range(d):
            s = s + q[j] * k[j]
        scores.append(s / math.sqrt(d))
    m = max(scores)
    e = [math.exp(s - m) for s in scores]
    t = sum(e)
    return [round(v / t, 4) for v in e]

practice.title: Forward diffusion step
practice.intro: Write noisy(x0, noise, alpha_bar): the noised sample x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar) x x0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar) x noise, elementwise on equal-length lists, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def noisy(x0, noise, alpha_bar):
    a = math.sqrt(alpha_bar)
    b = math.sqrt(1 - alpha_bar)
    return [round(a * x0[i] + b * noise[i], 4) for i in range(len(x0))]
